event.title: AHA Honors: Emmylou Harris, Will Kimbrough, Randy Owen, Fred Wesley
event.description:
Buy Tickets

Doors open at 5:30 p.m., show at 6:30 p.m.

On the stage of Birmingham’s historic Lyric Theatre, we’ll gather to celebrate the contributions of four iconic Alabama musicians to American storytelling and culture. Each honoree will share stories, and a selection of songs, from their careers.

Program highlights:

  • A short set of music, featuring songs performed by each of our newest Alabama Humanities Fellows: Emmylou Harris, Will Kimbrough, Randy Owen, and Fred Wesley
  • A conversation between our Fellows, moderated by Burgin Mathews, founding director of the Southern Music Research Center
  • Presentations of awards to our Fellows, by Allison Moorer (Harris), Kate Campbell (Kimbrough), the Hon. Nathaniel Ledbetter (Owen), and Dr. Henry L. Cobbs Jr. (Wesley)

About the Alabama Colloquium
Each year, the Alabama Humanities Alliance presents the Alabama Colloquium to celebrate how the humanities lift up our state and bring Alabamians together. We also bestow the title of Alabama Humanities Fellow on individuals whose outstanding work in the humanities has positively impacted our state, nation, and world. The event serves as annual fundraiser for the statewide work of the Alabama Humanities Alliance.

About the Alabama Humanities Alliance
Founded in 1974, the nonprofit and nonpartisan Alabama Humanities Alliance has served as a state affiliate of the National Endowment for the Humanities. AHA promotes impactful storytelling, lifelong learning and civic engagement. Through our programs and grantmaking, we provide Alabamians with opportunities to connect with each other, with our shared history, and with the vibrant and complex communities we call home. Learn more at alabamahumanities.org.

event.description:
Buy Tickets

Doors open 6:30 p.m., show at 7:30 p.m.

A show unlike any tribute you have ever seen or heard before. Broadway, television, and motion picture actor, Robert Neary creates a one of a kind, cut above the rest, production. He talks about the songs and tells stories behind them, from Neil’s interviews, quotes, and autobiographical books. You will swear you are watching the master himself, as he and the band perform 20 of Neil Diamond’s greatest hits. Songs like “Cherry Cherry”, “I Am, I Said”, “I’m a Believer”, “Solitary Man”, “Holly Holy”, “Coming to America”, “Sweet Caroline” and so many more. With a surprise finale that will leave you absolutely breathless, So Good! The Neil Diamond Experience is guaranteed to leave you speechless!

Born and raised in East Meadow, Long Island, NY, Robert Neary gained immediate success as an actor, when he was 20 years old, with a guest star role in the Television series “Fame”, and then opposite Jason Bateman in the film, “Teen Wolf Too”. He has since gone on to guest star in over 50 television shows, including “Criminal Minds”, “Sons of Anarchy”, “The Closer”, “Grey’s Anatomy”, ” Blue Bloods”, “Justified”, “The Fosters”, “FBI: Most Wanted”, “Weeds”, “Medium” “NCIS” and “NCIS New Orleans”. He landed his first Broadway show in 1996, starring in “Smokey Joe’s Café”, and then toured as the evil Zoser in Elton John’s Broadway hit “Aida”. He understudied the lead role of Sonny in the Broadway smash, “A Bronx Tale, The Musical”.

Robert grew up listening, mimicking, and creating his style to only 2 people in the music world. Elvis Presley and Neil Diamond. It has been a deep passion, to one day perform and put together a tribute show to Neil Diamond like none other. And here it is.

Comedian, New York Times Best Selling Author, Emmy-winning journalist, Billboard-topping musician and creator of the viral sensation, The Manitowoc Minute, Charlie Berens has announced the addition of 18 new dates to The Lost & Found Tour across North America in 2026, with a stop at Birmingham’s Lyric Theatre on November 6. His previous Good Old Fashioned Tour played 127 shows in 88 cities and was shot for his latest stand up special, “Neighborly,” a follow-up to 2023’s “Midwest Goodbye.”

This string of success has led to his New York Times Best Seller The Midwest Survival Guide being optioned for TV development and three sold out nationwide stand-up comedy tours. In his free time, Charlie hosts the hilarious “Bellied Up” podcast w/ “Myles The You Betcha Guy” where the two of them belly up at a small-town bar every Thursday and take live calls from all over the Midwest and rest of the world.  He also hosts “The Cripescast” podcast where he has meaningful conversations with a wide range of guests, including musicians, headlining comedians, dairy farmers, groundbreaking scientists, government officials, world-renown chefs, artists, business leaders, sports Hall of Famers, explorers, Olympians, and creators about their story and connections to the Midwest. He has amassed over 10 million followers and over 3 billion views across his social channels thanks to his relatable comedic sensibility and while grounded in Midwest culture, Charlie’s material consistently lands on a national level.

Additionally, Charlie became a Billboard Chart-topper in 2020 when he hit #1 on the Bluegrass chart for his music/comedy album Unthawed and an Emmy winner in 2013 for his piece “The Cost of Water” at KDAF in Dallas. He also finds time for charitable causes and most notably has served as the ambassador for Feeding America Eastern Wisconsin for three years. If that wasn’t enough, he even launched his very own brandy, Berens Old Fashioned Brandy, which is in stores now across Wisconsin. Throughout all his work, Charlie aims to connect with people through comedy and authenticity.

event.title: Author Book Signing with Kevin Morris
event.description:
On Saturday, October 10, the Birmingham Civil Rights Institute will welcome Kevin Morris for a book signing and discussion of his new book, An American Problem: How the Country Built—and the Supreme Court Broke—the Voting Rights Act.

An American Problem traces the rise and fall of the Voting Rights Act, from the triumph of its passage in 1965 to the Supreme Court’s 2013 decision in Shelby County v. Holder, which struck down a key provision of the law.

The book will be available for purchase in the BCRI Gift Store beginning October 6. With the midterm elections just weeks away, we’re looking forward to a timely conversation about the history, evolution, and state of the Voting Rights Act today.

Please register to let us know you’re coming.

About An American Problem: How the Country Built—and the Supreme Court Broke—the Voting Rights Act

The Voting Rights Act of 1965 finally made good on the promise of the Fifteenth Amendment, which nearly a century before had granted Black Americans the right to vote. The Voting Rights Act was the crowning achievement of the Civil Rights Movement, which had battled for years against voting laws that made it all but impossible for Black Americans to cast a ballot. The act was a resounding success, bringing Americans of all races and ethnicities into the democratic process. And then, in 2013, the Supreme Court brought this progress to a screeching halt with their decision in Shelby County v. Holder. In this book, Michael Miller and Kevin Morris offer a sweeping history of the Voting Rights Act and the attacks it has suffered.

Miller and Morris explain that central to the act’s success was its requirement that states and localities with a history of discrimination get federal permission to change their voting rules—a novel approach known as “preclearance.” It was this requirement that the Shelby County decision eviscerated. Miller and Morris trace the devastating effect of Shelby County, using advanced research techniques to prove that the decision unleashed racially discriminatory voting policies. The result is a nation in which Americans of color cast fewer ballots, and in which the ballots they do cast count for less. But the story does not end there: the Supreme Court continues to undermine what remains of the Voting Rights Act. What President Lyndon B. Johnson called “an American problem,” formerly kept in check by a strong federal law, once again threatens voting rights.

About the Authors

Michael G. Miller is professor of political science at Barnard College of Columbia University. He is the coauthor of Small Power and the author of Subsidizing Democracy. Kevin T. Morris is senior research fellow and voting policy scholar at the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University School of Law.

event.title: Author Book Signing & Discussion with Brian D. Goldstein
event.description:
Brian Goldstein, author of Max Bond: The Life and Work of the People’s Architect, will join us at the Birmingham Civil Rights Institute on Friday, October 30, at 12:00 p.m. for a book signing and discussion.

The first biography of Max Bond, the book explores the life and legacy of the civil rights activist, educator, and architect who championed the cause of freedom through architecture and helped shape Black history and modernism. Bond’s prolific portfolio includes the Martin Luther King, Jr. Center for Nonviolent Social Change in Atlanta, the Studio Museum in Harlem, and our very own Birmingham Civil Rights Institute.

Goldstein will begin with a brief overview of the book, followed by a panel discussion exploring historic places and spaces across Alabama and the importance of the built environment in preserving and telling our history.

Please register to let us know you’re coming.

About Max Bond: The Life and Work of the People’s Architect

J. Max Bond Jr. (1935–2009) was a civil rights activist, educator, and architect who shaped such iconic structures as the King Center for Nonviolent Social Change in Atlanta, the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, DC, and the 9/11 Memorial & Museum in Manhattan. Driven by the concerns of the civil rights movement, he insisted on a practice centered on deep social engagement during years when his profession became preoccupied with celebrity and spectacle.

Harvard educated and son of an eminent African American family, Bond designed housing, cultural institutions, community centers, and campuses amid an era of sweeping changes in architecture, urbanism, and American culture. He expressed an architectural vision that was democratic and inclusive, international in orientation, and celebratory of cities and their diverse residents. Yet his work has often been overlooked. Award-winning historian Brian Goldstein renders it visible.

Beautifully illustrated, Max Bond is the definitive biography of one of the most important architects of our time, whose aspiration toward an architecture by and for the people was as urgent in his day as it remains in our own.

About the Author
Brian D. Goldstein is an architectural and urban historian, and associate professor at Swarthmore College. His work focuses on the intersection of the built environment, race and class, and social movements, especially in the United States in the twentieth century. He is the author of Max Bond: The Life and Work of the People’s Architect. His first book, The Roots of Urban Renaissance: Gentrification and the Struggle Over Harlem, won the 2019 Lewis Mumford Prize for the Best Book in Planning History and the 2020 John Friedmann Book Award. He lives in Washington, DC.

event.description:
What do we choose to collectively remember, and how?

In this ArtBreak conversation, Tyler Jones, Director and founding member of 1504, and Joshua Jenkins, Mississippi and Alabama Field Representative for the National Parks Conservation Association, explore how a sense of place shapes individual and collective identity, and why preserving spaces where memory is embedded in the landscape matters. Drawing connections between The Sacred Ordinary, 1504’s public memory project, and Roll Call: Two Hundred Years of Black American Art, they will consider how art and storytelling can counteract erasure, deepen our understanding of history, and reveal the sacred within the ordinary. The program concludes with a brief gallery tour of Roll Call led by Jade Powers, Hugh Kaul Curator of Contemporary Art.

Tyler Jones is a filmmaker, experience designer, and founding member of 1504, a Birmingham-based narrative studio that integrates strategic communications with the visual arts. His recent projects include Joe Minter Is Here, a site-specific art installation honoring Birmingham artist Joe Minter, and In Solidarity: The Beth El Civil Rights Experience, an Emmy Award-nominated immersive exhibition exploring the Jewish community’s relationship to the Civil Rights Movement in Birmingham.

Joshua Jenkins is based in Birmingham and serves as Mississippi and Alabama Field Representative for the National Parks Conservation Association. His work supports national parks and heritage initiatives across Mississippi, Alabama, and South Carolina’s Lowcountry, focusing on the preservation of places that deepen our understanding of history and strengthen connections between communities and the landscapes they inhabit.

event.title: Air Supply: A Matter of Time Tour
event.description:
Buy Tickets
Plan Your Visit

Doors open at 6 p.m., show at 7 p.m.

Continuing to make musical history with every sold out performance around the world, legendary pop duo Air Supply is riding the wave of an eventful banner year in 2026, with concerts across North America, Australia, South America, Europe and Asia, a biopic in the works, an impending Star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and – brace yourselves, devoted Airheads – A Matter of Time, their first studio album in 15 years.

Graham Russell’s heartfelt and soul-piercing songwriting talents, along with his and Russell Hitchcock’s dynamic trademark vocals, are on emphatic display throughout the multi-faceted 11-track collection, due to drop digitally December 3, with the same release date for an exclusive special edition 80’s style vinyl version.

Released to coincide with Air Supply’s incredible 50th anniversary as a duo, A Matter of Time caps an historic career that compares to the Beatlesque feat of five consecutive Top Five Singles (“Lost in Love,” “All Out of Love,” “Every Woman in the World,” “The One That You Love,” “Here I Am”). During their early 80’s run, they sold a collective total of 20 million copies of their first three albums (Lost in Love, The One That You Love, Now & Forever) and the 1983 Greatest Hits collection and achieved multi-million radio plays for five of their hits, including “Sweet Dreams” and the Jim Steinman-penned “Making Love Out of Nothing At All.” In 2010, the year Air Supply released their last studio album Mumbo Jumbo, Graham was honored with a BMI Million-Air Certificate recognizing three million performances of “All Out of Love.”

“When it comes to our longevity, it’s sometimes hard to think about it, but Russell and I do often, usually while we’re traveling between cities,” says Graham. “You can never imagine being in a band or being an artist for that long, so it’s not easy to wrap your thoughts around it. When we started having some success, we thought we’d be around for a few years. Then as the years roll by, all of a sudden we’re at a half century since we met and people still enjoy hearing our songs and seeing us perform them.

“If I could pinpoint the reason,” he adds, “it’s because our music has never really been in style but it also never goes out of style. We’ve never followed any trends or been fashionable, but heartfelt love songs always seem to endure. And beyond simply making great records, we love hearing from fans around the world, particularly after our shows, saying things like, ‘God you have no idea what this song means to me or how it saved me from this or that.’ Having been a songwriter for over 64 years now, it’s particularly gratifying to hear that those songs I’ve written still resonate like that.”

The release of the album comes seven months after Graham and Russell celebrated a half century since meeting as chorus members of the Australian touring company of Jesus Christ Superstar in a most extraordinary way – headlining a sold-out show at Carnegie Hall on their actual 50th anniversary date.

The delirious fans in NYC lucky enough to attend their remarkable 5,560th show at Carnegie Hall might not have been aware of just how rare a feat it was, considering how resistant the powers that be often are to having pop-rockers play in a venue dominated by classical performances. With this concert, Air Supply rightfully joined a rarefied list of rock greats to have played the hallowed Hall, including The Rolling Stones, The Beach Boys, Chicago, Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd and Graham and Russell’s chief influences, The Beatles. This was a dream come true for the duo who both saw The Beatles perform in 1964 at different venues.

While most of the duo’s albums have been produced by Graham, the singer/songwriter was delighted to work this time with Grammy-nominated Canadian producer Brian Howes, a two time Juno Award, Dove Award and multiple BMI Award winner whose star-studded career includes recordings by the rock bands Skillet, Puddle of Mudd, Nickelback, Hedley and Simple Plan and tracks by American Idol greats Daughtry and David Cook.

A Matter of Time took a full two years to come together from inception to completed production for several reasons – Air Supply’s relentless ongoing 130 date U.S. and international annual tour schedule and Howes’ insistence, even in this digital age, that all of Graham and Russell’s vocals be recorded at his studio in Courtenay, Canada, an island off the coast of British Columbia, requiring several trips.

The duo also appreciated the opportunity to record the tracks old school, live in the studio with their band (drummer Pavel Valdman, lead guitarist Aaron McLain, keyboardist Mirko Tessandori and bassist Doug Gild), much the way Graham and Russell did in the early days, when he and Russell recorded their first albums in Australia, starting with their self-titled Top 20 Australian debut. In line with the possibility that A Matter of Time may be Air Supply’s final studio album (stay tuned!), Graham and Russell wanted the artwork to be special and sought out the talents of legendary Australian sculptor and painter Brett-Livingstone Strong to create the eye-popping, psychedelic time traveling artwork for the album, which includes an image of Air Supply circa 1981 amidst aliens, faeries, butterflies dinosaurs and cat-driven spaceships, among other colorful “easter eggs.”

“Brian is a great producer to work with, and we loved that he was always open to suggestions,” Russell Hitchcock says. “This creative partnership between myself, Graham and Brian led to a very mature album with great songs. Graham brings a different perspective on life to these tunes. When I sing, I think of different colors and there are so many that inspire me on A Matter of Time. Stylistically, I love the fact that there’s a great variance from track to track. I think the songs aren’t just ‘I love you and you love me’ and a chorus but lyrically very deep and thought provoking. I’m glad we’re releasing the album on vinyl so that fans can have a deeper appreciation for Graham’s storytelling as they listen.”

Graham adds, “Most artists recording tracks and albums now record one element at a time, then replace everything until it sounds good. “We appreciated the opportunity to create A Matter of Time live. There’s a certain spirit you get when that happens, and over the course of running through a dozen songs, if you’re patient, incredible sweet spots come that you couldn’t capture using a computer recording each musician separately. Our way is more fun and interactive, leading to trying out different notes, chords and overall approaches and ironing out the wrinkles. We ended up here with magic and when you’ve got that, you end up smiling!”

Air Supply audiences have already been smiling widely as the band performs the album’s symphonic, high spirited lead single “Wrap My Arms Around You” amidst their cavalcade of hits. Graham wrote the song during the pandemic, reflecting on the importance of physical human connection and a time when people would once again be able to hug their friends and loved ones without fear. Another of the duo’s favorites on the album is the soulful, haunting power ballad “If Only,” which features a mellotron element that pays subtle homage to the Fab Four’s “Strawberry Fields Forever.”

Other standouts include the raunchy, freewheeling Stones-influenced rocker “I Want Your Love,” the anthemic, hard-driving “Son of the Father” (from A Wall Apart, Graham’s stage musical about the Berlin Wall) and the passionate ballad “I Say A Prayer,” featuring Kennadi Dodds, a 22 year old, Utah-based singer/songwriter, who also contributed lyrics to the song.

“If someone had told us back in 1976 when we recorded our first album we would still be around, performing and recording stronger than ever, we would have told them they were insane,” Russell says. “These wonderful recent developments – playing the Hollywood Bowl and Carnegie Hall, the biopic, the Hollywood Walk of Fame – feel like a great stamp of approval from the media. But more importantly, they affirm the validity and continued relevance of our music.

“Love songs like ours will never go out of style because, when you think about it, at some point in everyone’s life, they’re falling in love, getting married, falling out of love or missing their love,” he adds. “Love is that constant that makes the world go round, and we’ve been sharing our songs about all those things with four generations now. I’ve said it a million times, the reason we keep playing is because of the songs. If you don’t have a song, you have nothing – and we’re excited now to share the new ones as we are to keep playing the classics.”

Gary Owen has been entertaining audiences for more than two decades with his sharp observational humor and fearless storytelling. Known for his unapologetic, rule-defying style, his material draws from his personal life, time in the military and the everyday absurdities that connect people across backgrounds. With a fanbase that has grown by the millions in recent months and continues to surge across social media, Owen’s reach has cemented his place as one of the most in-demand touring comedians today.

Beyond stand-up, Owen has appeared in a wide range of feature films including BACK ON THE STRIP with Tiffany Haddish and Wesley Snipes, MEET THE BLACKS and its sequel THE HOUSE NEXT DOOR, THINK LIKE A MAN and THINK LIKE A MAN TOO, RIDE ALONG with Ice Cube and Kevin Hart, LITTLE MAN opposite the Wayans Brothers, and DADDY DAY CARE with Eddie Murphy. He is also widely recognized for his scene-stealing role as “Bearcat” in the MGM film COLLEGE.

On television, Owen starred in his own BET series THE GARY OWEN SHOW and co-hosted TruTV’s sketch series UPLOAD WITH SHAQUILLE O’NEAL. After meeting Tyler Perry on THE TOM JOYNER MORNING SHOW, he was cast in the recurring role of Zach the barber on the TBS comedy series TYLER PERRY’S HOUSE OF PAYNE.

Owen continues to write, produce and perform his own groundbreaking comedy specials, including BLACK FAMOUS, #DOIN’ WHAT I DO, I GOT MY ASSOCIATES, I AGREE WITH MYSELF, TRUE STORY, URBAN LEGEND, and BREAKIN’ OUT THE PARK. Most recently, he recorded two specials back-to-back—BROKEN FAMILY and GARY OWEN…NO S, released this past spring on YouTube.

Date:  Oct 1st

Time: 5:00 PM – 8:00 PM

Location: 1107 Fulton St. ZARTONK Gallery

Armenian Cultural Month Celebration in cooperation with Downtown Fresno Partnership @ Mariposa Plaza. 

 

Landscape Memories, latitude 36.74773 / longitude 119.77237 (Fresno, CA)

On October 1, 2026, in Fresno, Antaramian Hofman exhibits the final artistic display of migratory footprints by way of dance and people gatherings. Artist Hazel Antaramian Hofman is recognized for her ‘artwork of traces’: art and writing that looks to movement and pathway as conceptual anchor points of expression.

The unknowingness of where you have been and where you are going is intrinsic to the movement of her pencil or the strokes of her paintbrush. Born in Armenia, now in Fresno, the pathway in between includes Moscow, Paris, New York, Boston, Madison, Kenosha, Milwaukee. For her, geographic coordinates share spaces with those who traverse them and those who document them.

In Spring 2026, Antaramian completed Step 2 of her project. A three-generation family of dancers in the Armenian tradition: Karine Nurijanyan, Anna Dolukhanyan, and Ani Sargsyan led viewer participants in an Armenian traditional dance placing their inked footprint upon the floored canvas as it served to cushion their trac

es of the event, the memory to come between themselves and the earth landscape. It became a marking of language and the line folk dance; all aimed at connection.

The traces of footprints and handprints are embedded further with the overlaid painting of Step 3 of Antaramian’s project, continuing to mark human physicality. A physicality that speaks to theindividual and the collective. Antaramian’s artistic and performance art traces are shared with other art motifs, such as birds, the sky, nondescript land, dystopic patterns, and shoes. The symbolic language of these motifs are terrestrial longings for flight.

event.title: Book Signing by David Karamian: Eternal Armenia: Khatchkars – The CrossStones of Noratus
event.description:
David Karamian will present his latest publication a new book, Eternal Armenia: Khatchkars – The CrossStones of Noratus, 

The book is the culmination of nearly three years of photography, research, writing, and design. It is a 264-page, large-format bilingual English-Armenian volume featuring nearly 200 photographs, documenting the ancient cemetery of Noratus near Lake Sevan—home to the world’s largest surviving collection of Armenian khatchkars.

Beyond the photography, the book explores the history of Christianity in Armenia, the evolution and symbolism of the khatchkar tradition, the master artisans who created these remarkable monuments, and the larger themes of faith, memory, resilience, and cultural preservation.

An important reason for creating the book was the urgency of preservation. Following the deliberate destruction of the historic Armenian cemetery of Julfa and the loss of thousands of irreplaceable khatchkars, Noratus has assumed even greater significance. Yet this extraordinary Armenian Christian and cultural treasure remains surprisingly little known, even within our own community.

Event will take place at the Armenian Museum of Fresno on Thursday October 8th, at 10 AM to 6 PM. 

David will be available to greet you at the museum and book signing.

event.title: Extraordinary Foods
event.description:
Extraordinary Foods was born in 2022 in Modesto, California, from a simple idea: ordinary food is easy to find—Extraordinary food is something you have to create.

Founded by Garret Bianco, Extraordinary Foods is a grassroots craft food company built around bold flavors, creativity, and a hands-on approach to making food from the ground up. What started with a passion for growing peppers and experimenting with hot sauce has grown into a unique food brand focused on sauces, condiments, fermented products, and custom food creations.

Garret began growing peppers in 2020, with a particular fascination for rare and exceptionally hot varieties. As his freezer began filling with peppers, he started turning them into hot sauces, experimenting with different combinations of heat, acidity, sweetness, smoke, fruit, and savory ingredients. The goal wasn’t simply to make something hot—it was to find the perfect balance in every bottle.

That philosophy became the foundation of Extraordinary Foods.

Based in the heart of California’s Central Valley, Garret draws heavily from the ingredients, agriculture, and character of the region. His creations incorporate locally inspired ingredients such as California figs, white grapes, Fresno and Anaheim peppers, Stanislaus tomatoes, Gilroy garlic, olive oil, and other California-grown products.

One of the company’s signature creations, California Figment, represents that philosophy. Developed over two years, the Central Valley-style BBQ sauce combines California white grapes and black Mission figs with peppers, garlic, tomatoes, vinegar, and savory ingredients to create a BBQ sauce that is distinctly Californian and anything but ordinary.

Extraordinary Foods has also expanded beyond its own product line into custom formulation and white-label production, helping other food businesses develop unique sauces and specialty products. One of the company’s most significant projects has been a custom Sciabica Charcuterie Sauce, created in partnership with the Sciabica family and their California olive oil company.

Garret’s work has also received attention beyond the local food community. Extraordinary Foods was featured on Good Day Sacramento, where Garret showcased California Figment and his craft sauce creations, putting a spotlight on the growing specialty-food scene in Modesto and the Central Valley.

At its core, Extraordinary Foods remains intentionally personal. It isn’t about becoming another mass-produced sauce company. It’s about craftsmanship, experimentation, local connections, and putting the creator’s time and passion into every product.

From rare peppers and fermentation to BBQ sauce, hot sauce, mustard, michelada mix, ponzu, and custom formulations, Extraordinary Foods is built on one belief:

Don’t make ordinary food. Make something Extraordinary.

Doors at 5; Food at 5:30 p.m.

event.title: Panel Discussion with Dr. Tracy Fisher & Curators Dr. Shannon Vittoria & Dr. Shipu Wang
event.description:
@

Long before their names faded from memory, Asian American artists were winning prizes, headlining exhibitions, and helping to shape modern American art. Join Tracy Fisher, Director of the Center for Social Justice & Civil Liberties and Drs. Shannon Vittoria and ShiPu Wang, curators of LACMA’s California Collectives: Asian American Moderns, 1924-1965 (on view at the Riverside Art Museum through November 1, 2026), as they bring to light this forgotten story from a period of U.S. history when discriminatory laws and “Yellow Peril” stereotypes cast immigrant and U.S.-born Asians as perpetual outsiders. Artists of Asian descent refused to be defined by xenophobia, as they exhibited alongside America’s canonical artists while organizing their own art collectives—welcoming friends of all backgrounds—and staging ambitious shows from San Francisco to Little Tokyo. Through their art, they told their own stories and claimed their place in American life. Discover a legacy of creativity, community, and belonging that’s finally getting the recognition it deserves.

event.description:
In September, our regular Mindfulness session with Christiane Wolf will be replaced by a Sound Bath led by Kris Matsuoka. Christiane returns on Wednesday, October 7.

Whether you are new to meditation or already have experience, we welcome you to this community sit in the beautiful A-Frame Theater of the Wende Museum’s Community Center. Each session is followed by complimentary garden refreshments and an optional movement class.

This Sound Bath is designed as a continuation of Christiane Wolf’s regular Wellness Wednesday session. We will begin together with a visualization for inner peace, followed by a guided relaxation of the body to help release tension, and finish by relaxing together to sound from live instruments tuned specifically to help you find peace. Please wear comfortable clothes. Floor space is limited for those who wish to lie down for the full experience, but you are welcome to bring a yoga mat, pillow, and blankets.

Teacher Bio:

Kris Matsuoka is a Los Angeles native and a graduate of Art Center College of Design in Pasadena. He lives and works in Culver City, California.

While working in the creative industry, Kris was always asked the same question: “How do you come up with your ideas?” That led to an ongoing exploration of a second question: “Where do ideas even come from?” Looking into the lives of his favorite artists and mentors, Kris found one common thread. They had all turned to meditation at some point, and discovered that “not knowing” is a nice place to be.

Through the practice of meditation, Kris has seen how it can sharpen our perception of the world and reconnect us with nature. Sound meditation has become his most recent area of focus. For the past decade, he has hosted Sound Baths, workshops, and classes that use sound to invoke a sense of wonder and help people relax. Kris has found that in a relaxed, free, and peaceful state, your best ideas come most clearly.

The stories we hear and see shape the world we live in. During these two free hands-on workshops, we will explore our relationships with media, technology, and popular culture. We will analyze media and create our own alternative messages with a focus on the ways environmental and climate justice impact our health.

These events are free for everyone. We are all part of a media ecosystem, whether we’re on social media, watching YouTube, reading articles, or sharing links with our friends and family. event.description:
Written by Wendy Kout and Michele Willens

Starring Wendie Malick, Charles Shaughnessy, Diedrich Bader and Charlie Adler

Today’s political pundits are predicting the upcoming midterms will determine the life or death of our democracy. But in 1950 a California Senate race also changed the world. It was then that a young Richard Nixon falsely accused his opponent, the beautiful, three term liberal congresswoman and ex-Broadway and opera star, Helen Gahagan Douglas, of being a Communist. Nixon earned the name “Tricky Dick,” Helen was dubbed the “Pink Lady.” He ascended to the Presidency… until Watergate. She was forgotten… until now.

The play is set in the past and the present, in Hollywood and Washington D.C., and builds to that dirty, dramatic Senate race while telling the cautionary personal tale of Helen, a flawed and remarkable heroine. It also gives us the compelling love story of the entertainment world’s first activist couple.

Don’t Blame Me, I Voted for Helen Gahagan Douglas is a warning and call to action for the upcoming November midterms.

event.description:
Join us for an evening of film, conversation, and community at the Wende Museum as we explore the stories we inherit, the identities we carry, and the unexpected connections that shape our world.

In The Bengali, named one of Nonfics’ Top 20 Documentaries, director Kavery Kaul takes an American woman to India to uncover the past of her grandfather, Shaik Mohamed Musa. He was one of the early group of men who arrived in the late nineteenth century and married African-American women. Her unlikely quest triggers a boldly different encounter between East and West. A personal search becomes a deeper journey into culture, memory, and identity, breaking barriers and building bridges, revealing how histories travel, and families form across unexpected places.

The Bengali has inspired the #UnderOurSun impact campaign, a digital storyteling movement that invites everyone to share their own cultural heritage and lived experience. Through in-person screenings, lively panel discussions, and digital storytelling, the campaign sparks timely conversation about migration and belonging.

The Alliance of Women Film Journalists calls The Bengali “a lyrical and poetic documentary that shows how stories and presumptions can change, forging connections that are rich and real — not just to the past, but to the world at large.”

In present times of political and ideological division and the rise of authoritarianism on a global
scale, the Wende Museum and the Thomas Mann House are launching a series of monthly
discussions for college and university students to be better able to understand and navigate these
changes and discourses. Topics under consideration include the crisis of truth; the contested
independence of academic and cultural institutions; and the power of narratives to conceptualize
change.

will prepare each session based on a few sources (texts, podcasts, videos). The final meeting will
take the form of a public workshop or panel discussion with specialists in the fields that were
touched on throughout the sessions. The participating students will have the opportunity to learn
about the field of cultural programming by having access to and close engagement with two
leading cultural organizations in Los Angeles. In addition, students will be able to attend
exclusive events at both the Thomas Mann House and the Wende Museum and learn about their
unique missions.

Starting in January 2027, the meetings will take place every last Friday of the month at 12pm at
the Wende Museum’s Community Center in Culver City. Complimentary lunch and drinks will
be provided.

If interested, please send an application letter to Oliver Hartmann (oliver.hartmann@vatmh.org)
and Joes Segal (jsegal@wendemuseum.org) before November 1, 2026, mentioning your
academic background (college or university and major) and a one-paragraph explanation of why
you would like to join this discussion series. Please mention “Student Council 2027” in the email
subject line.

event.description:
Join us for Samizdat Sundays—hands‑on textile workshops inspired by the spirit of creative resistance and DIY culture found in samizdat traditions. Each week offers a different project, connecting archival stories of subversion with contemporary making.

We encourage participants to bring an item each week—a T‑shirt, a pair of jeans, or any textile you’re ready to transform, repair, or experiment with.

Each session is free, open to all skill levels, and guided by artists who delight in subversion and play. Come for one or come for all—together we’ll stitch, alter, repair, and imagine new forms of expression.

Join us for Samizdat Sundays—hands‑on textile workshops inspired by the spirit of creative resistance and DIY culture found in samizdat traditions. Each week offers a different project, connecting archival stories of subversion with contemporary making.

October 4: From One to Many

Taking inspiration from Jan Sawka’s Invasion/Trees series, which was featured in the Undercurrents I show in 2023, we will tell a story through a series of three or more pieces that share the same elements but demonstrate a transformation. Sawka’s series began with a print of a tree in a landscape. Each piece in the series is based on this same image, yet each one is different, and a story is told through a growing red cloud or fog that seems to overtake the image as the pieces progress. We will not begin with prints, but can echo Sawka’s strategy by choosing an element (or two) that will appear in each of the pieces in our series. Perhaps your element will be a shape (circle, square, triangle, etc.) or a color (blue, purple, yellow, etc.), or a pattern or texture (textile works are welcome!). Begin with a shared element and see where the series/story takes you!

October 11: “OPEN AT YOUR OWN RISK”

Taking inspiration from Schaden (Damage), an artist magazine produced in East Berlin in the 1980s, we will make a sealed “magazine” that can only be read by cutting open the edges of the envelope that contains it. In exemplary samizdat fashion, Schaden magazines were handmade and limited in scope, with just 15 copies of each issue produced. The magazine contained poems, prints, charts, musings, photographs and ephemera, including pages made of foil and tissue paper. Hidden, secret, and filled with discarded and surprising materials…what’s not to love?!

We are approaching Days of the Dead and Halloween, times when many remember their lost loved ones. Perhaps your Schaden-style magazine is a memorial book to one you’ve lost (person, pet, idea, place, etc), or perhaps yours is a continuation of the series pieces we made last week. Like the Schaden magazines, ours will be an envelope with pages inside that are stapled/sewn/fixed on the binder side so that the envelope has to be cut open for the magazine to be read. We will have a collection of envelopes of various sizes, including some that are absurdly small and others that are quite large. Perhaps your Schaden-style magazine will fit in your back pocket; perhaps yours will need a custom-made envelope because it is so large. As always, see where these ideas lead you and go with it! Your envelope (and its contents) may be made of cloth, requiring an unraveling to open, or perhaps your envelope will be an idea of an envelope rather than a physical thing. Will yours have a warning on it, as I’ve titled this week’s project, or will yours have an invitation, like a bottle of potion in Alice’s Wonderland, asking someone to “Open Me?” Or perhaps yours will have only an address or no marks at all.

November 8: Moon Flags

The new exhibition, “Competing Cosmologies,” explores the intersection of art and science during the Cold War, a time of space exploration and interplanetary dreaming, when people were mistaking floating balloons for alien spaceships and writers, painters, and screenwriters were imagining clashes with martians and other creatures from far off galaxies (who almost always had bodies and faces that were similar to ours, with two eyes, two arms, and two legs), all while governments were in a race to put men (and dogs!) into space and onto the moon. The race to the moon was, apparently, in part a race to place a flag on the moon, which is what Buzz Aldrin did in 1969’s Apollo 11 mission, when he planted the United States flag (brought in a “flag transportation assembly”) on the moon before blasting off back to Earth. Aldrin later said that he suspected the flag was blown down during the blast off, but even if it still stands, it is most likely bleached out to white as some of the other nylon moon flags have done since, thanks to the powerful, unmitigated rays of the sun. The US has placed six flags so far and China has placed one (in 2020) and I think it’s interesting to imagine the flags turned into the white flags of surrender, as everything ultimately surrenders to the sun and the processes of decay inherent in our beautiful, life-giving universe.

For today’s workshop, we’re going to make a flag to honor our celestial companion. Will your moon flag be in reverence of the moon or possessive of it? Will your flag be hung above your moon altar or tucked into a box and kept on your fireplace mantle, unfurled, perhaps, when you light a fire, a replicant of the blazing sun, in your fireplace? What do you imagine a flag to be? The moon to be? Will your flag be bleached by the sun’s rays, as the moon appears to be, or will it be full of Earth’s colors? Your flag may be a shoulder patch or a paper collage, or a full-fledged patchwork or embroidered flag, or perhaps an idea of a flag, held in space by concept rather than a physical thing. Let’s bring the brilliant celestial body of our night sky down to earth today!

November 15: What Is Above Is Below

At the second-to-last regular season game at Dodgers Stadium this year, a wayward eared grebe flew into the game, landing on their belly in the center of the outfield. The grebe, it seemed, had mistaken the shiny green grass of the field for the aqueous plants on a placid lake, fooled by the day-for-night lights of the stadium, perhaps, as they made their migratory way to another part of the state. Fortunately, the poor fowl found their way out of the false pond and flew out of the stadium, presumably not much worse for their unfortunate belly flop.

I thought of this when I was thinking of project ideas around the new “Competing Cosmologies” exhibition, which explores the intersection of art and science during the Cold War. This global competition has led to countless satellites being sent into outer space, our constellations cluttered with competing, unmanned space contraptions, some pointing down spying eyes, others sending down internet signals to bring access to the most remote regions of the earth. There are companies that want to send tens of thousands of satellite mirrors into space that would turn day to night anywhere (with precision, they claim) by reflecting the sun’s light onto the earth. How confused will we all be once the sky is filled with satellites and mirrors, when one is not wishing on a star but a satellite, and when there is no longer any “night” at all to hold the night sky?

We truly can see that what is above is below. The trash of our world now fills the skies. But here at Samizdat, we know that “trash” may be transformed into treasure, so today, let’s work with our discarded materials to turn “trash” into a two-sided, or perhaps two-facing map that represents the skyscape above and the landscape we live on. Perhaps your “map” is like the sky-moon-stars body of the ancient Egyptian goddess Nut as portrayed in tombs, or perhaps yours is like the remarkable Skidi Pawnee star chart at the Field Museum in Chicago, an animal hide marked with all of the visible stars in the North American sky, or perhaps your map will be like the cluster of dots hovering above an animal figure in the cave at Lascaux. What happens when we bring the stars and moon down to earth and carry them in our pockets? What happens when we imagine the mountains and oceans in the universe, when we see their undulations and rhythms in the spaces between stars and on the surface of the moon? Day-for-night, night-for-day; signals going back and forth; material above, material below (and what is “above” and what is “below” in our wall-less, roofless universe anyway?)…these are all notions to ponder as you make your map.

About the teaching artist
Kate Ingold is an LA-based artist and poet working with the discarded, the damaged, and the worn out. Materials and methods include textiles, collage, photography, video, ceramics, and performative installation. She works in series driven by conceptual concerns and is currently making work in two interwoven projects: Relics for Future Rituals and Damaged Goods/Small Repairs.

event.description:
Join us for Samizdat Sundays—hands‑on textile workshops inspired by the spirit of creative resistance and DIY culture found in samizdat traditions. Each week offers a different project, connecting archival stories of subversion with contemporary making.

We encourage participants to bring an item each week—a T‑shirt, a pair of jeans, or any textile you’re ready to transform, repair, or experiment with.

Each session is free, open to all skill levels, and guided by artists who delight in subversion and play. Come for one or come for all—together we’ll stitch, alter, repair, and imagine new forms of expression.

Join us for Samizdat Sundays—hands‑on textile workshops inspired by the spirit of creative resistance and DIY culture found in samizdat traditions. Each week offers a different project, connecting archival stories of subversion with contemporary making.

October 4: From One to Many

Taking inspiration from Jan Sawka’s Invasion/Trees series, which was featured in the Undercurrents I show in 2023, we will tell a story through a series of three or more pieces that share the same elements but demonstrate a transformation. Sawka’s series began with a print of a tree in a landscape. Each piece in the series is based on this same image, yet each one is different, and a story is told through a growing red cloud or fog that seems to overtake the image as the pieces progress. We will not begin with prints, but can echo Sawka’s strategy by choosing an element (or two) that will appear in each of the pieces in our series. Perhaps your element will be a shape (circle, square, triangle, etc.) or a color (blue, purple, yellow, etc.), or a pattern or texture (textile works are welcome!). Begin with a shared element and see where the series/story takes you!

October 11: “OPEN AT YOUR OWN RISK”

Taking inspiration from Schaden (Damage), an artist magazine produced in East Berlin in the 1980s, we will make a sealed “magazine” that can only be read by cutting open the edges of the envelope that contains it. In exemplary samizdat fashion, Schaden magazines were handmade and limited in scope, with just 15 copies of each issue produced. The magazine contained poems, prints, charts, musings, photographs and ephemera, including pages made of foil and tissue paper. Hidden, secret, and filled with discarded and surprising materials…what’s not to love?!

We are approaching Days of the Dead and Halloween, times when many remember their lost loved ones. Perhaps your Schaden-style magazine is a memorial book to one you’ve lost (person, pet, idea, place, etc), or perhaps yours is a continuation of the series pieces we made last week. Like the Schaden magazines, ours will be an envelope with pages inside that are stapled/sewn/fixed on the binder side so that the envelope has to be cut open for the magazine to be read. We will have a collection of envelopes of various sizes, including some that are absurdly small and others that are quite large. Perhaps your Schaden-style magazine will fit in your back pocket; perhaps yours will need a custom-made envelope because it is so large. As always, see where these ideas lead you and go with it! Your envelope (and its contents) may be made of cloth, requiring an unraveling to open, or perhaps your envelope will be an idea of an envelope rather than a physical thing. Will yours have a warning on it, as I’ve titled this week’s project, or will yours have an invitation, like a bottle of potion in Alice’s Wonderland, asking someone to “Open Me?” Or perhaps yours will have only an address or no marks at all.

November 8: Moon Flags

The new exhibition, “Competing Cosmologies,” explores the intersection of art and science during the Cold War, a time of space exploration and interplanetary dreaming, when people were mistaking floating balloons for alien spaceships and writers, painters, and screenwriters were imagining clashes with martians and other creatures from far off galaxies (who almost always had bodies and faces that were similar to ours, with two eyes, two arms, and two legs), all while governments were in a race to put men (and dogs!) into space and onto the moon. The race to the moon was, apparently, in part a race to place a flag on the moon, which is what Buzz Aldrin did in 1969’s Apollo 11 mission, when he planted the United States flag (brought in a “flag transportation assembly”) on the moon before blasting off back to Earth. Aldrin later said that he suspected the flag was blown down during the blast off, but even if it still stands, it is most likely bleached out to white as some of the other nylon moon flags have done since, thanks to the powerful, unmitigated rays of the sun. The US has placed six flags so far and China has placed one (in 2020) and I think it’s interesting to imagine the flags turned into the white flags of surrender, as everything ultimately surrenders to the sun and the processes of decay inherent in our beautiful, life-giving universe.

For today’s workshop, we’re going to make a flag to honor our celestial companion. Will your moon flag be in reverence of the moon or possessive of it? Will your flag be hung above your moon altar or tucked into a box and kept on your fireplace mantle, unfurled, perhaps, when you light a fire, a replicant of the blazing sun, in your fireplace? What do you imagine a flag to be? The moon to be? Will your flag be bleached by the sun’s rays, as the moon appears to be, or will it be full of Earth’s colors? Your flag may be a shoulder patch or a paper collage, or a full-fledged patchwork or embroidered flag, or perhaps an idea of a flag, held in space by concept rather than a physical thing. Let’s bring the brilliant celestial body of our night sky down to earth today!

November 15: What Is Above Is Below

At the second-to-last regular season game at Dodgers Stadium this year, a wayward eared grebe flew into the game, landing on their belly in the center of the outfield. The grebe, it seemed, had mistaken the shiny green grass of the field for the aqueous plants on a placid lake, fooled by the day-for-night lights of the stadium, perhaps, as they made their migratory way to another part of the state. Fortunately, the poor fowl found their way out of the false pond and flew out of the stadium, presumably not much worse for their unfortunate belly flop.

I thought of this when I was thinking of project ideas around the new “Competing Cosmologies” exhibition, which explores the intersection of art and science during the Cold War. This global competition has led to countless satellites being sent into outer space, our constellations cluttered with competing, unmanned space contraptions, some pointing down spying eyes, others sending down internet signals to bring access to the most remote regions of the earth. There are companies that want to send tens of thousands of satellite mirrors into space that would turn day to night anywhere (with precision, they claim) by reflecting the sun’s light onto the earth. How confused will we all be once the sky is filled with satellites and mirrors, when one is not wishing on a star but a satellite, and when there is no longer any “night” at all to hold the night sky?

We truly can see that what is above is below. The trash of our world now fills the skies. But here at Samizdat, we know that “trash” may be transformed into treasure, so today, let’s work with our discarded materials to turn “trash” into a two-sided, or perhaps two-facing map that represents the skyscape above and the landscape we live on. Perhaps your “map” is like the sky-moon-stars body of the ancient Egyptian goddess Nut as portrayed in tombs, or perhaps yours is like the remarkable Skidi Pawnee star chart at the Field Museum in Chicago, an animal hide marked with all of the visible stars in the North American sky, or perhaps your map will be like the cluster of dots hovering above an animal figure in the cave at Lascaux. What happens when we bring the stars and moon down to earth and carry them in our pockets? What happens when we imagine the mountains and oceans in the universe, when we see their undulations and rhythms in the spaces between stars and on the surface of the moon? Day-for-night, night-for-day; signals going back and forth; material above, material below (and what is “above” and what is “below” in our wall-less, roofless universe anyway?)…these are all notions to ponder as you make your map.

About the teaching artist
Kate Ingold is an LA-based artist and poet working with the discarded, the damaged, and the worn out. Materials and methods include textiles, collage, photography, video, ceramics, and performative installation. She works in series driven by conceptual concerns and is currently making work in two interwoven projects: Relics for Future Rituals and Damaged Goods/Small Repairs.

Taco Tuesday at V’s Cellar

Taco Tuesday is back and better than ever! 🌮 Every Tuesday, we’re serving up our signature tacos, each bursting with bold, fresh flavors. Whether you’re craving our Al Pastor, the sweet & savory kick of Bulgogi Steak, the spicy tang of Korean Chicken, or the zest of Vegan Asian Ginger, we’ve got something for everyone. Plus, every taco is $1 off all day long!

Taco Tuesday is the perfect excuse to enjoy tacos for lunch, dinner, or a snack in between. Come indulge in your favorite fusion taco creations, and don’t forget: each week brings a new reason to come back for more! Whether you’re a Taco Tuesday regular or it’s your first time, we guarantee you’ll find something you love.

Mark your calendars, grab your friends, and make your Tuesday a little tastier with us!

event.title: Spreading Wings Gala
event.description:
Join Wings Over the Rockies for an unforgettable evening celebrating America’s premier flight demonstration team, the United States Air Force Thunderbirds!

The 2026 Spreading Wings Gala brings together aviation enthusiasts, community leaders, veterans, and business executives for one of Colorado’s premier events. Guests will enjoy an elegant evening featuring remarkable stories, exclusive experiences, and the highly anticipated unveiling of our fully restored Thunderbird F-16D.

The evening will feature a special conversation with our guest of honor, retired Brigadier General James Latham. A decorated combat pilot, former prisoner of war, and Thunderbird Commander, General Latham’s remarkable career is a testament to courage, leadership, perseverance, and service. His story reflects the values that have defined the Thunderbirds for generations and continue to inspire those who dream of taking flight.

The Thunderbirds represent excellence, precision, teamwork, and service. Their legacy extends far beyond the skies, inspiring future pilots, maintainers, engineers, astronauts, and innovators. Every ticket, sponsorship, and donation helps Wings Over the Rockies create life-changing opportunities that prepare young people to become the next generation of Thunderbirds.

At this event, you’ll experience:

  • Cocktail reception and elegant dinner
  • Keynote discussion with retired Brigadier General James Latham
  • Exclusive unveiling of our F-16D, painted in its original Thunderbirds livery
  • View 4 additional historic aircraft models flown by the Thunderbirds
  • Hear remarks from Thunderbirds Association Chair, Michael “Mo” Beale
  • Interact with Thunderbirds pilots, maintainers, and crews
  • Live auctions that include once-in-a-lifetime aviation adventures

Trust us, you don’t want to miss this remarkable evening honoring generations of aerospace excellence!

David Mamet’s Oleanna is an uncomfortably relevant play exploring gender, authority, power, and education through a series of increasingly fraught conversations between a university professor and his student. Written in 1992 in response to the Anita Hill–Clarence Thomas hearings, the play examines what happens when assumptions, personal biases, and failures of communication turn differences into divisions. The production invites audiences to reflect on their own perspectives and continue the conversation with openness and respect.

Join us on Thursday, Oct. 1, from 5–6:30 p.m. for a talkback and reception following that day’s 1 p.m. performance. Colorado College President Manya Whitaker will moderate the conversation. Refreshments and light hors d’oeuvres will be served. Talkback attendees may also receive a complimentary ticket to that evening’s performance of Come From Away, capacity permitting.

The talkback and reception are free and open to the public. RSVPs are strongly encouraged.

event.description:
In 2015, a James Bond movie introduced millions to a spectacularly staged Día de los Muertos parade in Mexico City. Two years later, the Pixar movie Coco depicted some of the rituals associated with the Day of the Dead. But did you know that the Mexico City parade didn’t exist until the filmmakers created it? Or that Disney, in anticipation of Coco’s release, filed an application to trademark the phrase “Día de los Muertos” to sell merchandise? What does the actual observance look like, and has it always looked that way? Through a series of images, this lecture travels across Mexico to uncover the many regional traditions behind one of the world’s most recognizable commemorations. Peel back the Hollywood imagery to explore a family of living practices shaped by Indigenous ritual, Spanish Catholicism, and sometimes, even the movies.

This lecture coincides with the FAC annual community event Día de Muertos, on November 1 and 2.

Themed Cocktail: Muertos Margarita
Lecturer: José Antonio Arellano, Associate Professor of English, United States Air Force Academy

Friday, October 2, 2026

Punch needle is a traditional craft that’s been around since the 15th century. Initially known as the ‘punch stitch,’ it was primarily used for adorning religious garments. It was also a craft used by men during lengthy sea voyages who would create punched rugs to pass the time between ports.

Imagine your hands immersed in colorful Shaker wool as you create your own punch needle trivet or hot plate. You’ll be using 2-ply Shaker yarn which has been spun from virgin wool from the sheep on our farm which include Romney, Shropshire, Icelandic, North Country Cheviot and Finnsheep breeds.

Instructor, artist and punch needle enthusiast, Bonnie Faulkner, will teach you the basics. Threading the Lavor punch needle, a hollow, pencil-shaped needle used to push yarn through fabric, creating tufted loops that result in an embroidered-like surface will be a breeze.

This is a perfect workshop for a beginner or those who have tried punch needle and would like a bit more guidance on technique. All materials and design options will be provided. If you have any special 2-ply wool from home you’d like to use, please bring it!

Punch needle is a wonderful craft to digitally disconnect, switch off, and relax from a busy and stressful life.

Class size: 10

Saturday, October 3, 2026
10am-3pm

In this in-person class with Kathryn Polletto of Kennebunk Basketry, participants will make a Market Basket, a very functional basket for carrying various items. This basket measures 6″ x 12″ x 5 1/2″, when completed, with an Oak handle that measures 6″x 10″. The basket is made with various widths of reed splint and five strands of hand-dyed reed will be added for some color and pattern.

The participant will learn the first steps of making a rectangular basket with a closed bottom. The participant will learn how to weave up the sides, finish off the top, and lash on a rim.

Level: This basket is good for beginners or for those who have some knowledge of basket weaving.

Students will bring from home:
-Basin or Bucket for water
-yard stick or tape measure
-heavy scissors
-pencil
-spray bottle
-awl or knitting needle
-spring clothespins
-small towel

All basket reeds and materials will be supplied.

Class size: Minimum 5, Maximum 8

Kathy Polletto has been weaving baskets for over 40 years. She began weaving because she was very interested in 18th century history and she admired how utilitarian, everyday items were handmade with such skill. Basket making particularly intrigued her as she enjoyed working with natural fibers such as plant and wood-based materials. She is essentially self-taught. She learned by reading books, as well as by visiting historical sites and craft fairs to observe other craftsmen weaving. Eventually, she joined High Country Basketry Guild in Virginia. There she was able to learn other techniques working with other basket weavers. Kathy has a Facebook page and Instagram page under Kennebunk Basketry. She sells her baskets at Shaker Village.

Turn off the noise and tune into all your senses on a slow, mindfulness guided walk through the 150 acre Shaker Bog with Certified Forest Therapy Guide, Nev Hoffman of Blue Fern Forest Bathing.

We will be exploring Shaker thoughts from Sister Ada S. Cummings, Sister R. Mildred Barker, and others throughout history and experiencing the diverse eco-system of the Shaker Bog through guided mindfulness invitations. Session concludes with a “Sharing Tea” in the forest where we can soak up our experience with a final tasting sensory experience of Shaker tea and treats.

The many well researched health benefits include slowing your pulse, lowering blood pressure, improving natural immune system, lowering stress, and increasing creativity…to name a few.

Nev will be greeting people starting 1/2 hour ahead of class time behind the Shaker Store.

Lightweight portable tripod camp chairs provided.

Please dress in layers for the weather. Rain jackets and umbrellas encouraged in case of rain.

Event is rain or shine. A note: rain is a sensory delight, but high winds/storms are not safe! We will announce via email and social media of a high winds weather cancellation.

Please bring/wear bug repellent if desired. We will have some on hand, too.

Bring a water bottle and a blanket, if desired.

We love our furry friends, but please no dogs allowed for this group guided session in order to ensure a comfortable and mindful experience for you and for others.

Please note there are bathrooms at Shaker Village, but not on the Bog.

3 hour session begins and ends in Shaker Village. Space is limited.

Nev Hoffman of Blue Fern Forest Therapy

Meet your guide, Nev Hoffman of Blue Fern Forest Bathing, Certified Forest Bathing Guide

Many people ask me: “Isn’t Forest Bathing just like walking in the woods?” And that’s exactly what I thought too, that is, until I tried it.

After 25 years as a full time photographer, I had a series of transformative life experiences during the pandemic that brought me to the Japanese practice of “Shinrin Yoku,” or Forest Bathing. Despite having spent my entire life in the woods, after just a few guided Forest Bathing sessions it’s like my eyes were opened and I was full immersed and experiencing nature for the first time.

I noticed for hours and even days after a session I felt calm, grounded, and peaceful. I knew the forest accepted me and that I had found home again.

I’m a tea geek, and another aspect of guided forest bathing that caught my imagination was the tea gathering at the end of each session.

All these experiences led me to get certified through The Forest Therapy School and to launch Blue Fern so I could share this meditative outdoor wellness practice and all it’s health benefits with the world.

I hope to meet you soon and have tea in the forest together.

Nev Hoffman

Education Programs

Plan Your Visit

Kids & Families

Classes

Classes

On the 2nd Saturday of each month, we hold a hands-on event for families with children ages 5-12. Activities include art projects, interactive programs and Museum-wide events. Reservations are not required, but seating is available on a first come, first served basis. The Museum supplies all materials and activities are included with regular Museum admission.

Contact the education department (209) 940-6315 or education@hagginmuseum.org for more information.

Visit our events page for a listing of 2nd Saturday classes.

Students & Teachers

Little ones art tour

Little ones art tour

This interactive tour for children from preschool to 1st grade introduces little ones to the museum and uses a variety of activities to engage young viewers. It is suitable for one class of 20—30 children at a time. The one-hour tour includes:

  • Introduction to the museum
  • A conversation about art elements
  • Guided look at paintings in the Haggin Collection
  • Storytelling
  • Hands-on art project


Tours

How to book a tour or program

How to book a tour or program

If you are interested in booking a tour or program, please fill out the Request Form in its entirety and e-mail it to education@hagginmuseum.org at least three weeks in advance of your desired date. During certain times of the year, tours are in high demand and availability may be limited. Request forms will be processed in the order they are received, and it make take up to 2 business weeks for your request to receive a response. If you have any questions, please contact the Education Department at (209) 940-6332.

 

We can accommodate up to 60 children per one-hour tour at the museum. If your group is larger than that, we will make arrangements for additional tours. Plan to bring at least one adult per 10  children for your tour. The tour group may only be in the building during the hour booked for the tour. We do not have room to accommodate waiting groups inside the museum.

Docent Volunteers

Volunteer Docent Training

Haggin Museum Docents make connections with visitors, students, art & history, the community, and more! Join our community of docents—today!


Docents Application

Docent

Haggin Museum docents provide a valuable service on behalf of the museum by leading tours, guiding visitors on the weekends, leading programs in school classrooms, helping with special events, and much more.

Application

 Participation in the Docent Program at the Haggin provides opportunities for continuing education and personal growth through field trips, training, tours, guest lectures, and a variety of social events. As a part of the team at a world-class museum, docents build a supportive community of colleagues and friends as they give back to the community through education. Interested in becoming a docent?


Download The Application

Haggin Museum Education Department

The Haggin Museum Education Department is proud to serve our community with trained volunteer docents who provide free museum tours and school site programs. On occasion, we welcome high school and college volunteers to help with family programs and workshops.

Contact

Participants must become museum members and pay a materials fee for each training course. Both history and art training are approximately 12 weeks each. The weekly classes meet on Tuesdays at the Haggin Museum. Please contact the Education Department at (209) 940-6315 or education@hagginmuseum.org for more information.

Docent-led Tours

Docent-led Tours

Docent-led tours feature themes that have been developed in conjunction with grade appropriate curriculum content. They unite exhibits in both the art and history galleries under big ideas while accommodating student interests.


Learn more about tours

Acorn making – 3rd grade

Acorn making •  3rd Grade

This hands-on program shares the importance of the acorn to Native People with pictures, acorn pounding, a sequencing activity, and a game of chance.

Looking at horses in art – 3 – 4th grade

Looking at horses in art •  3 – 4Th Grade

Docents introduce the theme of horses in art using images from the Haggin Collection and other museums. Then they lead an interactive discussion making connections between time periods and cultures and the students’ own experiences. The program concludes with a drawing lesson.

Looking at Young People in art – 5 – 8th grade

Looking at Young People in art •  5 – 8th Grade

Docents present a digital slide show and conduct an interactive discussion about the depiction of young people, their families, friends, and feelings in art. Additionally, the class creates an expressive self-portrait.

Mysteries – 3 – 4th grade

Mysteries  •  3 – 5TH Grade

History’s Mysteries is presented by Docents in your classroom or after-school program. Students learn about California history using objects circa 1900 and relating them to items used today. The program was used direct observation, a game and activity.

Making space – 3 – 7th grade new!!!

Making Space  •  3 – 7TH Grade New!!

Making Space explores how artists create the illusion of space in art with a digital slide show and conversation. Students learn how technique contributes to the meaning of the art and use their understanding of pictorial space to create landscape drawings of their own.

event.title: Inspiring Stowe: The Real Josiah Henson
event.description: On this tour, we explore how Harriet Beecher Stowe came to author Uncle Tom’s Cabin (1852), a complex and controversial anti-slavery novel with a massive impact on U.S. history and culture. We’ll discover what Stowe learned, read, and witnessed that made her want to speak out against enslavement in her own time, with special attention to the life of Josiah Henson, the real-life Black abolitionist who inspired the character of Tom in Stowe’s novel.

event.title: Writing Freedom
event.description:
Enter Harriet Beecher Stowe’s 1870’s historic home, where we’ll make space for powerful stories from history.

What is a Freedom Narrative? Historically referred to as a “slave narrative,” a freedom narrative is a true, firsthand account of liberation by a Black storyteller, describing their efforts to free themselves from slavery and to build a life in freedom. Thousands of freedom narratives were written, dictated, and shared before and after slavery legally ended in the United States. Their creators used the power of their words to speak out against injustice, assert their humanity, and record the truth of our nation’s history.

On this tour, we’ll learn about three 19th-century Black abolitionists: Harriet Jacobs, Frederick Douglass, and Josiah Henson. Each of these authors had a direct connection to and impact on the writing of Harriet Beecher Stowe, but this tour focuses on their lives and activism. We’ll have the opportunity to hear portion of their stories, told in their own words, and to consider the lessons these stories hold for our own time.
